text: Why don't I criticize Latter-day Saint
scripture? Hey everybody, I'm Dan
McClellan. I'm a scholar of the Bible
and religion and I'm frequently asked
why I don't turn my critical eye on
Latter-day Saint scripture. And this is
usually an attempt to try to accuse me
of being biased towards Latter-day
Saints or Latter-day Saint ideologies
and of only criticizing the Bible. But
the Bible is Latter-day Saint scripture
and the overwhelming majority of the
things I critique in the Bible apply
equally to Latter-day Saint ideologies
and doctrines. And I have repeatedly and
consistently pointed out that the data
don't really support an ancient origin
for the Book of Mormon or the veracity
or historicity of Latter-day Saint truth
claims and specifically supernatural
truth claims. So, I am not giving
Latter-day Saints a pass, but uniquely
Latter-day Saint scripture is not my
academic specialization. However, I did
spend a just over a decade as a
scripture translation supervisor for the
LDS Church and I have published and
presented research that critiques
widespread and long-standing Latter-day
Saint interpretations and ideologies.
And I'll just share two of them in this
video. The first is based on a passage
from the Book of Mormon 2 Nephi 25:23.
And down at the bottom here it says,
"For we know that it is by grace that we
are saved after all we can do." And
throughout the majority of the 20th
century, this passage was leveraged to
indicate that we have to do all we can
before grace kicks in and can result in
our salvation.
And in 2020, I published in the Journal
of Book of Mormon Studies this paper, 2
Nephi 25:23 in literary and rhetorical
context, which is freely available
through my link tree. But what this
paper demonstrates conclusively is that
this phrase "after all we can do" was
widely used in the late 18th and early
19th centuries even in discussions about
the role of grace in salvation and
invariably
it was used to mean despite all we can
do. And so 2 Nephi 25:23 when it was
originally published would have been
interpreted by readers to mean we are
saved by grace despite all we can do.
And another passage that I have
addressed in a conference presentation
was Doctrine and Covenants 138. And this
is a passage that has been used to
indicate that the voice of God's
servants is isometric with God's own
voice. In other words, whatever God's
servants, and this is widely understood
to mean the prophets, the leadership of
the church say is what God would say.
There's no daylight between the two of
them. And here's this passage. It says,
"What I the Lord have spoken I have
spoken and I excuse not myself. And
though the heavens and the earth pass
away, my words shall not pass away, but
shall all be fulfilled whether by mine
own voice or by the voice of my servants
it is the same." And it's those last two
lines that are frequently quoted.
"Whether by mine own voice or by the
voice of my servants it is the same."
And the idea here is that my own voice,
the voice of my servants, they're the
same voice. And in this YouTube video,
which is from two years ago, I point out
that the antecedent of it is the main
question here. And the antecedent is not
the two voices. The antecedent is the
fulfillment of what God has said. And
so, it's actually saying whether what I
have said is fulfilled by my own voice
or fulfilled by the voice of my
servants, it is fulfilled all the same.
And in that presentation, I demonstrate
that my servants doesn't just refer to
the leadership of the church, it refers
primarily to missionaries. And that the
context here is the spreading of the
gospel. And so, the fulfillment of God's
word is achieved through the preaching
of the gospel. So, when it says,
"Whether it is fulfilled by mine own
voice or by the voice of my servants,"
that's talking about the spreading of
the gospel and that fulfillment is what
is the same whether it is done by my
voice or by the voice of my servants.
And that is
a challenge to a more contemporary and
more authoritative reading that is still
frequently appealed to from the pulpit
during general conference and things
like that. So, again, I have
consistently and repeatedly pointed out
that the data don't support the
supernatural truth claims of the LDS
Church including the historicity or an
ancient origin for the Book of Mormon.
And I have published critiques of
popular, even authoritative
interpretations of Latter-day Saint
scripture in the past. But it's not
really a big part of my channel because
my channel is about the Bible and
religion and it is for a more general
audience. And so, that is why you're not
going to see me talk about Latter-day
Saint scripture very much at all on my
channel. And the fit for this video has
been the Spawn number one cover.
